The black-and-yellow rockfish (Sebastes chrysomelas) reaches a maximum recorded total length of 39 centimeters [Li = 39 centimeters], a value that positions it as a moderately sized member of the genus Sebastes along the California coast. Individuals attaining this ultimate length are typically long-lived and exhibit the robust body plan characteristic of nearshore rockfishes inhabiting rocky reef habitats. Field surveys conducted among the kelp forests and low-relief boulder fields of central California have consistently shown that the species rarely surpasses this asymptotic size, suggesting that growth decelerates markedly once the fish approach this upper boundary. The allometric relationship between length and body mass for this species, derived from a large sample of dissected individuals across multiple size classes, reveals that an adult fish at this maximum length carries a wet weight of approximately 825 grams [Wwi = approximately 825 grams], reflecting the deep-bodied morphology typical of benthic rockfishes.

Sexual maturation in the black-and-yellow rockfish is a gradual process tied to both size and environmental temperature. Individuals first attain puberty at a total length of about 15 centimeters [Lp = about 15 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 43 grams [Wwp = roughly 43 grams] according to the species-specific length-weight conversion. This pubertal size is reached relatively early in the ontogeny of the species, enabling first reproduction to occur before the full adult body mass is achieved. In the thermally stable subtidal environment where this rockfish resides, the age at which puberty occurs is closely linked to the prevailing water temperature; a significant body of work has examined these relationships at a stable thermal regime of 16.7 °C [T = 16.7 °C], which approximates the annual mean temperature of the species' core rocky-reef habitat.

The reproductive output of black-and-yellow rockfish reflects an iteroparous strategy typical of temperate scorpaenids. Females extrude large clutches of fertilized eggs during the winter spawning season, and the maximum reproductive rate achieved under favorable feeding conditions is quite substantial. At the population's typical thermal environment of 16.7 °C, each female produces approximately 425,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 425,000 eggs per spawning event], with roughly one spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per year]. This pattern yields a total annual fecundity of approximately 425,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 425,000 eggs per year]. This daily reproductive output is a direct consequence of the viviparous reproductive mode, wherein females internally fertilize and then release live larvae rather than demersal eggs. The high fecundity partially compensates for the considerable larval mortality that occurs during the pelagic dispersal phase.

The larval stage of this species begins with a surprisingly small birth mass. Newly extruded larvae have a wet weight of roughly 0.000268 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000268 grams], a value derived from the spherical volume of the 0.8 millimeter diameter egg prior to fertilization and approximately three orders of magnitude lower than the asymptotic adult mass, reflecting the extreme fecundity necessary to offset high larval mortality in the planktonic environment. This minute starting mass characterizes the yolk-sac larva, which is lecithotrophic and relies entirely on its finite yolk reserves for the first several days of exogenous existence. The rapid transition to first exogenous feeding is therefore critical, as any delay in encountering suitable planktonic prey can push the larva past the point of no return. Despite the energetically constrained start, survivors grow quickly through the flexion and postflexion stages, with the larval-juvenile transition occurring after several weeks of active feeding in the water column.

Longevity in black-and-yellow rockfish is notably high for a fish of its body size. At the stable environmental temperature of 16.7 °C [T = 16.7 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years], a value that aligns with the broader life-history pattern observed in many slow-growing rockfishes of the eastern Pacific. This extended lifespan, combined with delayed senescence, allows multiple reproductive seasons across the adult phase and contributes to the species' resilience in fluctuating environments. Age determination based on otolith increment analysis from museum specimens corroborates this longevity estimate, with the oldest individuals recorded from protected sites within marine reserves showing the full 22-year span.
